summary: EarthPulse is an interactive web platform designed to visualize floods and changes in water bodies, utilizing principles from the NASA–ISRO NISAR radar mission, with a focus on Oman. Users can navigate an interactive map, toggle through time-aligned layers (including validated NISAR data from October 21, 2026), and utilize an Analyze feature to compare water extent changes between two selected dates, which updates the map accordingly. The current version features illustrative map layers based on SAR water detection methods, which identify low backscatter over open water. Users can access real, validated NISAR products for free through ASF Vertex and NASA Earthdata. EarthPulse tackles the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by making complex radar data concepts more accessible through visual tools. It promotes environmental awareness and education, aids in initial flood assessments, and provides a clear pathway from open NASA–ISRO data to interpretable information for communities, students, and researchers.
details:
What does it do & how does it work?

EarthPulse is an interactive web application focused on Oman. Users explore a map of water-related layers (baseline, 21 October 2026, change detection, flood-prone zones), adjust opacity, and use a Compare & Analyze tool: they select a start date and an end date, click Analyze, and receive a summary of illustrative water-extent change while the map updates to the change layer. The app is designed around NISAR radar concepts (especially L-band sensitivity to open water and inundation) and links the idea of open NASA–ISRO data to a simple browser experience.

Benefits:

It makes complex radar observations easier to understand without specialized software. Users can visually explore where water coverage may have changed, support basic flood awareness, and connect to real NISAR data sources (ASF Vertex and NASA Earthdata) for further work.

Intended impact:

Improve public and educational understanding of floods and water change; support students, teachers, and local communities in Oman; and demonstrate a practical path from open NISAR products to accessible digital tools for environmental awareness and preliminary assessment.

Tools and technologies:

HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Leaflet.js for the interactive map, GeoJSON for illustrative water layers, and static hosting (Netlify). The prototype is browser-based and requires no backend. Future development can incorporate processed NISAR GCOV products and Python-based analysis.

Creativity:

The project turns dual-frequency SAR science into a simple, local-first experience: date comparison, visual change summary, and an Oman-centered map that anyone can open. It bridges official open data with a clear user interface rather than requiring users to process radar files themselves.

Factors considered:

Feasibility as a prototype within the hackathon timeframe; focus on a specific region (Oman); alignment with validated NISAR data availability from 21 October 2026; clarity for non-experts; open technologies; and honesty that current map layers are illustrative while real NISAR products remain freely available for deeper analysis.
